what_it_does: Databases store huge tables on disk (or in storage devices), and a common query operation is filtering rows based on conditions — for example, keeping only rows where a price column falls between two values. Normally the storage device just delivers the raw data and the server CPU applies the filter, transferring far more data than will actually be used. In-storage processing (doing computation inside the storage device itself) can eliminate most of that wasted transfer, but prior in-storage designs only handle simple equality or range comparisons on basic column types, not the complex filter expressions real analytical databases use. UPP defines a compact set of instructions specifically designed for expressing filter conditions of arbitrary complexity, separate from any particular storage hardware. The database software translates a filter expression into these instructions and ships them to a programmable chip (an FPGA — a chip whose logic can be reconfigured in the field) inside the storage device. That chip evaluates the filter directly on the stored data, using compact metadata to skip irrelevant sections, and only sends back rows that pass, without needing to reformat the data on disk.
